paper_topic: Fit Cards: query-conditioned structured metadata for agentic marketplace search at large consideration sets

nodes.text: As large language models become capable of autonomous economic action, a new paradigm of agentic commerce is emerging where AI agents search, negotiate, and transact on behalf of human principals (Rothschild et al., 2025).
This shift promises efficiency gains through automated discovery and negotiation, but introduces fundamental challenges in marketplace design.

When agents must evaluate large consideration sets—hundreds of potential sellers matching a customer's query—they face an information bottleneck that human-designed interfaces were never built to address.
nodes.display_label: Info bottleneck at large consideration sets

nodes.text: The core problem is that marketplace search results typically present truncated natural language descriptions that lose critical fit signals.

A customer seeking specific menu items, amenities, and budget constraints cannot reliably determine from a 40-token description snippet whether a restaurant carries the requested dishes or falls within budget.

At scale, this information loss compounds: agents contact businesses based on incomplete signals, accumulate irrelevant context from poor-fit interactions, and exhibit first-proposal bias that locks in suboptimal early matches (Bansal et al., 2025).
In our experiments with 100 businesses, the baseline system achieves only 7.8% contacted-fit rate—agents waste over 90% of their interactions on businesses that cannot satisfy customer requirements.
A natural hypothesis is that agent-side interventions—better prompting or more inference compute—can overcome this information bottleneck.
Our experiments reject this hypothesis.

Prompting agents to explicitly extract fit signals from truncated descriptions actually hurts welfare, dropping it from 68.51 to −35.85: agents become more selective but without sufficient information to act on, leading to misdirected selectivity.

Inference scaling fares no better: providing 4.7× more LLM calls and forcing agents to explore multiple options yields negative welfare (−29.71) because additional computation cannot recover information lost during description truncation.
These failures reveal that the bottleneck is information, not reasoning capacity.
We propose Fit Cards, a platform-side intervention that replaces truncated descriptions with query-conditioned structured metadata.

Rather than presenting generic text snippets, the platform computes fit signals—how many requested items are available, which amenities match, and the estimated price—directly from its structured catalog.
Results are sorted by relevance with explicit rank labels, enabling agents to identify high-fit businesses at a glance.
In experiments on a restaurant marketplace with 100 businesses, Fit Cards achieve 11.4× higher welfare than the status quo baseline while using 28% fewer LLM calls.

We identify the information bottleneck in agentic marketplace search, showing that agent-side interventions fail because truncated descriptions lose fit signals that agents cannot recover through reasoning.
We propose Fit Cards, a platform-side intervention that surfaces query-conditioned structured metadata computed from the platform's catalog.
We demonstrate that Fit Cards improve contacted-fit rate from 7.8% to 73.6%, validating that better discovery-stage contact selection drives welfare improvements.
We show that discovery-stage interventions are more effective than proposal-stage interventions: first-proposal bias persists but does not dominate welfare when agents contact high-fit businesses.

observations:
FA0214 is a marketplace-design paper anchored on the Magentic Marketplace simulation framework. Para 1 (N1-N6) is dense Context: agentic commerce paradigm, the design challenges it raises, the information bottleneck at large consideration sets, truncated descriptions losing fit signals, the 40-token snippet failure mode, and how loss compounds at scale via first-proposal bias (Bansal 2025). N7 is a Result-as-evidence: the 7.8% baseline contacted-fit rate quantifies the bottleneck.

Para 2 introduces a 'natural hypothesis' Prior_Work N8 (agent-side interventions like prompting or inference scaling) followed by Limitation N9 ('our experiments reject this hypothesis') with two Result nodes (N10 prompting drops welfare to -35.85; N11 inference scaling -29.71). N9 has Prior_Work N8 as its required upstream source (PW->L contrast). Limitation N12 ('bottleneck is information, not reasoning') unfolds from the same critique chain (N11 elaboration; upstream PW source via N8 -> N9 -> N12 chain through N11).

Method block (N13-N15) introduces Fit Cards (platform-side metadata, computed fit signals, sorted with rank labels). N16 reports the headline 11.4x welfare result. Four Contributions (C1-C4) close the intro with addresses edges to the two Limitations: C1, C2 -> N12 (information bottleneck framing); C3, C4 -> N9 (the rejected agent-side hypothesis). N16 forks into all four contributions; N9 and N12 are join targets.
